fp1_roots_coefficients.description: Read root sums, pair and triple products from coefficients. Reconstruct a polynomial and count repeated roots consistently.

sections.title: Why divide by the leading coefficient first?
sections.label: Normalise and compare
sections.intro: Writing a quadratic as \(a(x-\alpha)(x-\beta)\) separates its leading multiplier from the roots. Dividing by that multiplier simplifies comparison.

blocks.html: \((x-\alpha)(x-\beta)=x^2-(\alpha+\beta)x+\alpha\beta\). Match the coefficients after dividing by \(a\).

blocks.title: Read the two root quantities without solving
blocks.prompt: The roots of \(3 x^{2} - 5 x - 6=0\) are \(\alpha,\beta\). Find their sum and product.

retry.feedback: The sign of the x coefficient reverses.

blocks.hint: Compare with the expansion of two factors, including the signs.
blocks.solution:
Divide every coefficient by the leading coefficient to get \(x^{2} - \frac{5 x}{3} - 2=0\).

The x coefficient is minus the sum of the roots, giving \(\alpha+\beta=\frac{5}{3}\).

The constant term is their product, so \(\alpha\beta=-2\).

blocks.html: A leading multiplier affects every coefficient. Dividing only the first term changes the equation.

sections.title: Why are there three different root quantities for a cubic?
sections.label: Compare the three coefficient positions
sections.intro: A term in the expanded product takes either the variable or the negative root from each factor. Choosing one, two or three roots gives alternating signs.

blocks.html: For a monic cubic, the squared coefficient is minus \(\sum\alpha\), the linear coefficient is \(\sum\alpha\beta\) and the constant is minus \(\alpha\beta\gamma\).

blocks.title: Read sums and product from a non-monic cubic
blocks.prompt: The roots of \(3 x^{3} - 2 x^{2} + 7 x - 4=0\) are \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\). Find the sum of roots, the sum of their pair products and their product.

retry.feedback: The constant of a monic cubic is minus the product.

blocks.hint: Read the squared, linear and constant coefficients in that order.
blocks.solution:
The monic polynomial is \(x^{3} - \frac{2 x^{2}}{3} + \frac{7 x}{3} - \frac{4}{3}\). The coefficients give the alternating signs.

Read \(\sum\alpha=\frac{2}{3}\) from the squared term and \(\sum\alpha\beta=\frac{7}{3}\) from the linear term.

The constant is minus the product, so \(\alpha\beta\gamma=\frac{4}{3}\).

blocks.html: The pair-product sum includes each of the three unordered pairs once. It is different from squaring the sum.

sections.title: Where do the triple products go in a quartic?
sections.label: Use four coefficient slots
sections.intro: The three non-leading powers and the constant each have their own root relation. Count all pairs and triples of distinct root positions.

blocks.html: In a quartic the coefficient of \(x\) is minus the triple-product sum after normalisation. The constant gives the product of all four roots.

blocks.title: Keep all four slots of a quartic
blocks.prompt: Find the sum of the roots, sum of pair products, sum of triple products and product of all four roots of \(4 x^{4} - 2 x^{3} - 3 x^{2} + 3 x + 6=0\).
blocks.hint: Leave a zero coefficient in the list when a power is missing.
blocks.solution:
Use the coefficient of \(x^3\) for the root sum and of \(x^2\) for the pair products. They give \(\frac{1}{2}\) and \(- \frac{3}{4}\).

The coefficient of \(x\) gives minus the triple-product sum after division by the leading coefficient. It gives \(- \frac{3}{4}\).

The constant gives four negative factors, so the product of all four roots is \(\frac{3}{2}\).

blocks.html: Do not slide the coefficient list left when a power is missing. That power has coefficient zero.

blocks.title: Keep all four slots of a quartic
blocks.prompt: Find the sum of the roots, sum of pair products, sum of triple products and product of all four roots of \(6 x^{4} - 4 x^{3} - 5 x^{2} + 5 x + 8=0\).
blocks.hint: Leave a zero coefficient in the list when a power is missing.
blocks.solution:
Use the coefficient of \(x^3\) for the root sum and of \(x^2\) for the pair products. They give \(\frac{2}{3}\) and \(- \frac{5}{6}\).

The coefficient of \(x\) gives minus the triple-product sum after division by the leading coefficient. It gives \(- \frac{5}{6}\).

The constant gives four negative factors, so the product of all four roots is \(\frac{4}{3}\).

blocks.html: Check that the degree, number of root positions and number of coefficient conditions agree.

sections.title: Does a repeated root count twice?
sections.label: Keep all root positions
sections.intro: A repeated value can occur in two distinct factor positions. In the cubic \((x-u)^2(x-v)\), the first two positions have the same value.

blocks.html: For roots \(u,u,v\), the sum is \(2u+v\), the pair sum \(u^2+2uv\) and the product \(u^2v\).

blocks.title: Use the ordering to select the repeated root
blocks.prompt: A monic cubic has roots \(u,u,v\) with \(v>u>0\). Their sum is \(10\) and the sum of their pair products is \(28\). Find \(u,v\) and the monic polynomial.

retry.feedback: This candidate makes v smaller than u.

blocks.hint: Keep both algebraic candidates until you check the ordering.
blocks.solution:
The first condition gives \(v=10 - 2 u\). The pair products include \(u^2\) once and \(uv\) twice.

Substitute into the pair-product condition to solve \(3 u^{2} - 20 u + 28=0\). The candidates for \(u\) are \(2\) and \(\frac{14}{3}\).

The second gives \(v=\frac{2}{3}\), so it violates \(v>u\). The accepted values are \(u=2\) and \(v=6\). The polynomial is \(x^{3} - 10 x^{2} + 28 x - 24\).

blocks.html: When solving for the repeated value, check all algebraic candidates against the stated ordering.

sections.title: How do I go from root relations to an equation?
sections.label: Write the monic polynomial
sections.intro: The root relations reverse direction: once they are known you can write the coefficients without solving for individual roots.

blocks.html: Start with the correct degree. Fill the remaining positions in descending powers with signs negative, positive, negative and, for a quartic, positive.

blocks.title: Build the monic cubic from three root relations
blocks.prompt: For a monic cubic the sum of roots is \(3\), the sum of pair products is \(-6\), and their product is \(-8\). Enter its monic polynomial in \(x\).
blocks.hint: A monic cubic is determined by the three root relations. Put the alternating signs in before expanding.
blocks.solution:
The coefficient of \(x^2\) is the negative of the root sum \(3\).

The coefficient of \(x\) is \(-6\). The constant is minus \(-8\).

Assemble the terms to get \(x^{3} - 3 x^{2} - 6 x + 8\).

blocks.html: Only a non-zero common multiplier preserves the whole equation’s roots. Keep the polynomial monic when requested.

blocks.title: Build the monic cubic from three root relations
blocks.prompt: For a monic cubic the sum of roots is \(5\), the sum of pair products is \(-12\), and their product is \(-36\). Enter its monic polynomial in \(x\).
blocks.hint: A monic cubic is determined by the three root relations. Put the alternating signs in before expanding.
blocks.solution:
The coefficient of \(x^2\) is the negative of the root sum \(5\).

The coefficient of \(x\) is \(-12\). The constant is minus \(-36\).

Assemble the terms to get \(x^{3} - 5 x^{2} - 12 x + 36\).

examples.title: Read the two root quantities without solving
examples.question: The roots of \(2 x^{2} - 3 x - 5=0\) are \(\alpha,\beta\). Find their sum and product.
solution: Divide every coefficient by the leading coefficient to get \(x^{2} - \frac{3 x}{2} - \frac{5}{2}=0\).
The x coefficient is minus the sum of the roots, giving \(\alpha+\beta=\frac{3}{2}\).
The constant term is their product, so \(\alpha\beta=- \frac{5}{2}\).

examples.title: Read sums and product from a non-monic cubic
examples.question: The roots of \(2 x^{3} + x^{2} + 5 x + 3=0\) are \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\). Find the sum of roots, the sum of their pair products and their product.
solution: The monic polynomial is \(x^{3} + \frac{x^{2}}{2} + \frac{5 x}{2} + \frac{3}{2}\). The coefficients give the alternating signs.
Read \(\sum\alpha=- \frac{1}{2}\) from the squared term and \(\sum\alpha\beta=\frac{5}{2}\) from the linear term.
The constant is minus the product, so \(\alpha\beta\gamma=- \frac{3}{2}\).

examples.title: Keep all four slots of a quartic
examples.question: Find the sum of the roots, sum of pair products, sum of triple products and product of all four roots of \(3 x^{4} - x^{3} + 2 x^{2} + 5=0\).
solution: Use the coefficient of \(x^3\) for the root sum and of \(x^2\) for the pair products. They give \(\frac{1}{3}\) and \(\frac{2}{3}\).
The coefficient of \(x\) gives minus the triple-product sum after division by the leading coefficient. It gives \(0\).
The constant gives four negative factors, so the product of all four roots is \(\frac{5}{3}\).

examples.title: Keep all four slots of a quartic
examples.question: Find the sum of the roots, sum of pair products, sum of triple products and product of all four roots of \(5 x^{4} - 3 x^{3} + 4 x^{2} + 4 x + 7=0\).
solution: Use the coefficient of \(x^3\) for the root sum and of \(x^2\) for the pair products. They give \(\frac{3}{5}\) and \(\frac{4}{5}\).
The coefficient of \(x\) gives minus the triple-product sum after division by the leading coefficient. It gives \(- \frac{4}{5}\).
The constant gives four negative factors, so the product of all four roots is \(\frac{7}{5}\).

examples.title: Use the ordering to select the repeated root
examples.question: A monic cubic has roots \(u,u,v\) with \(v>u>0\). Their sum is \(6\) and the sum of their pair products is \(9\). Find \(u,v\) and the monic polynomial.
solution: The first condition gives \(v=6 - 2 u\). The pair products include \(u^2\) once and \(uv\) twice.
Substitute into the pair-product condition to solve \(3 u^{2} - 12 u + 9=0\). The candidates for \(u\) are \(1\) and \(3\).
The second gives \(v=0\), so it violates \(v>u\). The accepted values are \(u=1\) and \(v=4\). The polynomial is \(x^{3} - 6 x^{2} + 9 x - 4\).

examples.title: Build the monic cubic from three root relations
examples.question: For a monic cubic the sum of roots is \(6\), the sum of pair products is \(-1\), and their product is \(-30\). Enter its monic polynomial in \(x\).
solution: The coefficient of \(x^2\) is the negative of the root sum \(6\).
The coefficient of \(x\) is \(-1\). The constant is minus \(-30\).
Assemble the terms to get \(x^{3} - 6 x^{2} - x + 30\).

examples.title: Build the monic cubic from three root relations
examples.question: For a monic cubic the sum of roots is \(3\), the sum of pair products is \(-10\), and their product is \(-24\). Enter its monic polynomial in \(x\).
solution: The coefficient of \(x^2\) is the negative of the root sum \(3\).
The coefficient of \(x\) is \(-10\). The constant is minus \(-24\).
Assemble the terms to get \(x^{3} - 3 x^{2} - 10 x + 24\).

glossary.definition: Leading coefficient equal to one.
Number of times the factor associated with a root occurs.
\(\sum\alpha\) adds every root position.
\(\sum\alpha\beta\) adds products of unordered pairs of positions.
\(\sum\alpha\beta\gamma\) adds products of unordered triples of positions.

revision.checks:

  • The pair-product sum includes each of the three unordered pairs once. It is different from squaring the sum.
revision.examTip: Normalise first and count with multiplicity. Use a discriminant or another argument if reality has to be established.

related.title: Symmetric functions of roots and power sums

fp1_roots_symmetric_sums.description: Use S₁, S₂ and S₃, reciprocal identities and recurrences to evaluate symmetric functions without solving for each root.

sections.title: How do I get the sum of squares from coefficients?
sections.label: Remove the mixed products
sections.intro: A power sum \(S_k=\sum_i r_i^k\) adds the kth powers of all root positions. The subscript gives a power, while \(\sum\alpha\beta\) describes products of different positions.

blocks.html: \(S_2=S_1^2-2\sum\alpha\beta\). Each cross term occurs twice in the expansion of \(S_1^2\).

blocks.title: Subtract the doubled pair products
blocks.prompt: For the roots of \(x^{3} - 4 x^{2} - 11 x + 30=0\), calculate \(S_2\) without solving the cubic.

retry.feedback: Subtract the pair products counted twice in the square of the sum.

blocks.hint: The square of the sum also contains pair products.
blocks.solution:
Read \(S_1=4\) and \(\sum\alpha\beta=-11\) from the coefficients.

In \(S_1^2\) each pair product occurs twice. Remove those mixed terms using \(S_2=S_1^2-2\sum\alpha\beta\).

The answer is \(S_2=38\).

blocks.html: Do not confuse \(S_2\) with \(\sum\alpha\beta\). Read the pair-product sum from the coefficient and then apply the identity.

sections.title: How do the pair products help find the sum of cubes?
sections.label: Combine the first three root quantities
sections.intro: For a cubic, comparing the terms in the product of the first and second power sums produces a relation involving the pair products and the product of all three roots.

blocks.html: \(S_3=S_1S_2-(\sum\alpha\beta)S_1+3\alpha\beta\gamma\). The last term accounts for the three product contributions.

blocks.title: Combine square and pair sums to get cubes
blocks.prompt: The roots of \(x^{3} - 4 x^{2} - 11 x + 30=0\) are \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\). Find \(S_2\) and \(S_3\).
blocks.hint: Compute the pair-product sum and full product before using the cube identity.
blocks.solution:
Read \(S_1=4\), \(\sum\alpha\beta=-11\), and \(\alpha\beta\gamma=-30\).

First \(S_2=38\) from \(S_1^2-2\sum\alpha\beta\).

The cube identity \(S_3=S_1S_2-(\sum\alpha\beta)S_1+3\alpha\beta\gamma\) then gives \(S_3=106\).

blocks.html: Dropping the triple-product term can significantly change the answer, including its sign.

sections.title: What do I check before taking reciprocals?
sections.label: Use a non-zero full product
sections.intro: The constant term detects a zero root. If no root is zero, work with a common denominator equal to the product of all roots.

blocks.html: For cubic roots the reciprocal sum is \(\frac{\sum\alpha\beta}{\alpha\beta\gamma}\) and the reciprocal pair sum is \(\frac{S_1}{\alpha\beta\gamma}\). Apply the square-sum identity to get \(S_{-2}\).

blocks.title: Find reciprocal square sums using one denominator
blocks.hint: For reciprocals, first check that the original constant term is non-zero.
blocks.solution:
The constant is non-zero, so every root is non-zero. With the common denominator \(\alpha\beta\gamma=-30\), the reciprocal sum is \(\frac{11}{30}\).

The reciprocal pair-product sum is \(- \frac{2}{15}\). Its numerator is the sum of the original roots.

Now apply the same square identity to reciprocal roots to obtain \(S_{-2}=\frac{361}{900}\).

blocks.html: A reciprocal identity cannot be used if any original root is zero.

blocks.title: Find reciprocal square sums using one denominator
blocks.hint: For reciprocals, first check that the original constant term is non-zero.
blocks.solution:
The constant is non-zero, so every root is non-zero. With the common denominator \(\alpha\beta\gamma=14\), the reciprocal sum is \(\frac{23}{14}\).

The reciprocal pair-product sum is \(\frac{5}{7}\). Its numerator is the sum of the original roots.

Now apply the same square identity to reciprocal roots to obtain \(S_{-2}=\frac{249}{196}\).

blocks.html: For four non-zero roots the numerator of the reciprocal sum is the sum of triple products.

sections.title: How can I calculate a higher power sum efficiently?
sections.label: Multiply and sum the root equation
sections.intro: Write the equation at a single root. Multiplying by a power of that root gives a relation you can sum over every root.

blocks.html: \(ar^3+br^2+cr+d=0\) leads to \(aS_{k+3}+bS_{k+2}+cS_{k+1}+dS_k=0\) for \(k\ge0\). Use \(S_0=3\) for a cubic.

blocks.title: Read a recurrence from the equation each root satisfies
blocks.prompt: For \(x^{3} - 3 x + 3=0\), find \(S_3\) and \(S_6\) using the root equation.

retry.feedback: The constant in the root equation is counted once for each of the three roots.

blocks.hint: The starting value S₀ counts every root position.
blocks.solution:
At a root \(r\), \(r^3=3 r - 3\). Multiplying by \(r^k\) and summing gives \(S_{k+3}=3S_{k+1}-3S_k\).

Start with \(S_0=3,S_1=0\) and \(S_2=6\). Therefore \(S_3=-9\).

The next values are \(S_4=18\) and \(S_5=-45\). Use \(S_4\) and \(S_3\) to obtain \(S_6=81\).

blocks.html: The constant occurs once for each root when \(k=0\). Dropping this factor gives a wrong starting value.

sections.title: Can power sums determine a cubic?
sections.label: Work backwards through the identities
sections.intro: If a monic cubic has its first three power sums specified, work back to the root sum, pair-product sum and product. These are three independent coefficient values.

blocks.html: Use \(S_2\) to recover the pair sum first. Then rearrange the \(S_3\) identity to obtain the product without solving the equation.

blocks.title: Recover coefficients from power-sum data
blocks.prompt: A monic cubic has \(S_1=4\), \(S_2=38\) and \(S_3=106\). Find the pair-product sum, product and monic polynomial.
blocks.hint: Work backwards from second and third powers to the elementary quantities, in that order.
blocks.solution:
Solve \(S_2=S_1^2-2\sum\alpha\beta\) for the pair-product sum. It is \(-11\).

Next rearrange the cube identity for the product. It is \(-30\).

Use the reconstructed root sum, pair-product sum and product to write \(x^{3} - 4 x^{2} - 11 x + 30\).

blocks.html: Do not put the second and third power sums directly into the polynomial. Convert them to root products first.

blocks.title: Recover coefficients from power-sum data
blocks.prompt: A monic cubic has \(S_1=10\), \(S_2=54\) and \(S_3=352\). Find the pair-product sum, product and monic polynomial.
blocks.hint: Work backwards from second and third powers to the elementary quantities, in that order.
blocks.solution:
Solve \(S_2=S_1^2-2\sum\alpha\beta\) for the pair-product sum. It is \(23\).

Next rearrange the cube identity for the product. It is \(14\).

Use the reconstructed root sum, pair-product sum and product to write \(x^{3} - 10 x^{2} + 23 x - 14\).

examples.title: Subtract the doubled pair products
examples.question: For the roots of \(x^{3} - 3 x^{2} - 6 x + 8=0\), calculate \(S_2\) without solving the cubic.
solution: Read \(S_1=3\) and \(\sum\alpha\beta=-6\) from the coefficients.
In \(S_1^2\) each pair product occurs twice. Remove those mixed terms using \(S_2=S_1^2-2\sum\alpha\beta\).
The answer is \(S_2=21\).

examples.title: Combine square and pair sums to get cubes
examples.question: The roots of \(x^{3} - 3 x^{2} - 6 x + 8=0\) are \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\). Find \(S_2\) and \(S_3\).
solution: Read \(S_1=3\), \(\sum\alpha\beta=-6\), and \(\alpha\beta\gamma=-8\).
First \(S_2=21\) from \(S_1^2-2\sum\alpha\beta\).
The cube identity \(S_3=S_1S_2-(\sum\alpha\beta)S_1+3\alpha\beta\gamma\) then gives \(S_3=57\).

examples.title: Find reciprocal square sums using one denominator
examples.question: For the roots of \(x^{3} - 3 x^{2} - 6 x + 8=0\), find \(S_{-1}\) and \(S_{-2}\).
solution: The constant is non-zero, so every root is non-zero. With the common denominator \(\alpha\beta\gamma=-8\), the reciprocal sum is \(\frac{3}{4}\).
The reciprocal pair-product sum is \(- \frac{3}{8}\). Its numerator is the sum of the original roots.
Now apply the same square identity to reciprocal roots to obtain \(S_{-2}=\frac{21}{16}\).

examples.title: Find reciprocal square sums using one denominator
examples.question: For the roots of \(x^{3} - 8 x^{2} + 9 x + 18=0\), find \(S_{-1}\) and \(S_{-2}\).
solution: The constant is non-zero, so every root is non-zero. With the common denominator \(\alpha\beta\gamma=-18\), the reciprocal sum is \(- \frac{1}{2}\).
The reciprocal pair-product sum is \(- \frac{4}{9}\). Its numerator is the sum of the original roots.
Now apply the same square identity to reciprocal roots to obtain \(S_{-2}=\frac{41}{36}\).

examples.title: Read a recurrence from the equation each root satisfies
examples.question: For \(x^{3} - 2 x - 3=0\), find \(S_3\) and \(S_6\) using the root equation.
solution: At a root \(r\), \(r^3=2 r + 3\). Multiplying by \(r^k\) and summing gives \(S_{k+3}=2S_{k+1}+3S_k\).
Start with \(S_0=3,S_1=0\) and \(S_2=4\). Therefore \(S_3=9\).
The next values are \(S_4=8\) and \(S_5=30\). Use \(S_4\) and \(S_3\) to obtain \(S_6=43\).

examples.title: Recover coefficients from power-sum data
examples.question: A monic cubic has \(S_1=3\), \(S_2=21\) and \(S_3=57\). Find the pair-product sum, product and monic polynomial.
solution: Solve \(S_2=S_1^2-2\sum\alpha\beta\) for the pair-product sum. It is \(-6\).
Next rearrange the cube identity for the product. It is \(-8\).
Use the reconstructed root sum, pair-product sum and product to write \(x^{3} - 3 x^{2} - 6 x + 8\).

examples.title: Recover coefficients from power-sum data
examples.question: A monic cubic has \(S_1=8\), \(S_2=46\) and \(S_3=242\). Find the pair-product sum, product and monic polynomial.
solution: Solve \(S_2=S_1^2-2\sum\alpha\beta\) for the pair-product sum. It is \(9\).
Next rearrange the cube identity for the product. It is \(-18\).
Use the reconstructed root sum, pair-product sum and product to write \(x^{3} - 8 x^{2} + 9 x + 18\).

extraPractice.prompt: For the roots of \(x^{3} - 8 x^{2} + 9 x + 18=0\), calculate \(S_2\) without solving the cubic.

retry.feedback: Subtract the pair products counted twice in the square of the sum.

extraPractice.hint: The square of the sum also contains pair products.
extraPractice.solution:
Read \(S_1=8\) and \(\sum\alpha\beta=9\) from the coefficients.

In \(S_1^2\) each pair product occurs twice. Remove those mixed terms using \(S_2=S_1^2-2\sum\alpha\beta\).

extraPractice.title: Combine square and pair sums to get cubes
extraPractice.prompt: The roots of \(x^{3} - 8 x^{2} + 9 x + 18=0\) are \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\). Find \(S_2\) and \(S_3\).
extraPractice.hint: Compute the pair-product sum and full product before using the cube identity.
extraPractice.solution:
Read \(S_1=8\), \(\sum\alpha\beta=9\), and \(\alpha\beta\gamma=-18\).

First \(S_2=46\) from \(S_1^2-2\sum\alpha\beta\).

The cube identity \(S_3=S_1S_2-(\sum\alpha\beta)S_1+3\alpha\beta\gamma\) then gives \(S_3=242\).

extraPractice.title: Find reciprocal square sums using one denominator
extraPractice.hint: For reciprocals, first check that the original constant term is non-zero.
extraPractice.solution:
The constant is non-zero, so every root is non-zero. With the common denominator \(\alpha\beta\gamma=-20\), the reciprocal sum is \(\frac{19}{20}\).

The reciprocal pair-product sum is \(- \frac{1}{10}\). Its numerator is the sum of the original roots.

Now apply the same square identity to reciprocal roots to obtain \(S_{-2}=\frac{441}{400}\).

extraPractice.title: Read a recurrence from the equation each root satisfies
extraPractice.prompt: For \(x^{3} - x - 3=0\), find \(S_3\) and \(S_6\) using the root equation.

retry.feedback: The constant in the root equation is counted once for each of the three roots.

extraPractice.hint: The starting value S₀ counts every root position.
extraPractice.solution:
At a root \(r\), \(r^3=r + 3\). Multiplying by \(r^k\) and summing gives \(S_{k+3}=1S_{k+1}+3S_k\).

Start with \(S_0=3,S_1=0\) and \(S_2=2\). Therefore \(S_3=9\).

The next values are \(S_4=2\) and \(S_5=15\). Use \(S_4\) and \(S_3\) to obtain \(S_6=29\).

extraPractice.title: Recover coefficients from power-sum data
extraPractice.prompt: A monic cubic has \(S_1=2\), \(S_2=42\) and \(S_3=62\). Find the pair-product sum, product and monic polynomial.
extraPractice.hint: Work backwards from second and third powers to the elementary quantities, in that order.
extraPractice.solution:
Solve \(S_2=S_1^2-2\sum\alpha\beta\) for the pair-product sum. It is \(-19\).

Next rearrange the cube identity for the product. It is \(-20\).

Use the reconstructed root sum, pair-product sum and product to write \(x^{3} - 2 x^{2} - 19 x + 20\).

glossary.definition: \(S_k=\sum_i r_i^k\) counts each root position.
A quantity unchanged by reordering the roots.
Products of different root positions, each unordered pair once.
A negative power, defined only for non-zero roots.
A rule giving a later power sum from earlier ones.

fp1_roots_transformations.description: Find equations whose roots are translated, scaled, reciprocal, squared or related by another algebraic substitution.

sections.title: Why do I substitute the inverse rule?
sections.label: Express the old variable in terms of the new
sections.intro: The transformation describes the values you want. The original equation contains the old variable, so rearrange the transformation before putting it into the original polynomial.

blocks.html: If \(y=mx+h\) with \(m\ne0\), use \(x=\frac{y-h}{m}\). Multiply by \(m^n\) to remove the constant denominators for degree \(n\).

blocks.title: Use the inverse affine substitution
blocks.prompt: Let the old roots belong to \(x^{3} - 4 x^{2} - 11 x + 30=0\). Find the monic polynomial in \(y\) for the transformed roots defined by \(y=3 x - 1\).
blocks.hint: Substitute for x, not for y. Clear constant denominators at the end.
blocks.solution:
Rearrange the rule for the original variable: \(x=\frac{y}{3} + \frac{1}{3}\).

Substitute this into the old polynomial, then multiply by \(27\) to restore the monic leading coefficient.

Expansion gives \(y^{3} - 9 y^{2} - 120 y + 700\). Each new root comes from exactly one old root because the multiplier \(3\) is non-zero.

blocks.html: Adding to the roots means subtracting that addition in the substitution for the old variable.

sections.title: Why do reciprocal roots reverse coefficients?
sections.label: Clear the highest inverse power
sections.intro: For a reciprocal transformation first check that zero is not an original root. Then the substitution \(x=\frac1y\) gives negative powers of the new variable.

blocks.html: For degree \(n\), form \(y^nP\left(\frac1y\right)\). The old constant becomes the new leading coefficient.

blocks.title: Reverse coefficients after checking zero
blocks.prompt: For the roots of \(x^{3} - 4 x^{2} - 11 x + 30=0\), find the monic polynomial in \(y\) whose roots are their reciprocals.
blocks.hint: Each coefficient reverses its place after multiplication by the highest power of the new variable.
blocks.solution:
The original constant is non-zero. Put \(y=\frac1x\) so \(x=\frac1y\).

Multiplication by \(y^3\) gives \(30 y^{3} - 11 y^{2} - 4 y + 1=0\). The new constant is non-zero, so the excluded value \(y=0\) is not added.

Divide by \(30\) to obtain the monic polynomial \(y^{3} - \frac{11 y^{2}}{30} - \frac{2 y}{15} + \frac{1}{30}\).

blocks.html: If a root at zero is defined in the output polynomial, check that it is not introduced by clearing denominators.

sections.title: How do I keep repeated images after squaring?
sections.label: Replace the even power
sections.intro: Squaring can send two distinct roots to one value. The transformed polynomial should still have one factor per old root position.

blocks.html: \((-1)^nP(x)P(-x)\) is even for monic degree \(n\). Its factor for each old root \(r\) is \(x^2-r^2\). Put \(y=x^2\).

blocks.title: Square roots without losing repetitions
blocks.prompt: Find the monic polynomial in \(y\) whose roots are the squares of the roots of \(x^{3} - x^{2} - 9 x + 9=0\), counting multiplicity.
blocks.hint: Retain a factor for every original root position, even when two images coincide.
blocks.solution:
The polynomial factors as \(\left(x - 3\right) \left(x - 1\right) \left(x + 3\right)\). In particular the roots \(3\) and \(-3\) have the same square.

Their squares are \(9\), \(9\) and \(1\). The first value occurs twice.

Multiply the factors \(\left(y - 9\right)^{2} \left(y - 1\right)\), obtaining \(y^{3} - 19 y^{2} + 99 y - 81\). An alternative without factorisation is to replace \(x^2\) by \(y\) in \(-P(x)P(-x)\).

blocks.html: If you use a squared relation to remove a variable another way, justify that every new root has the required origin and multiplicity.

blocks.title: Square roots without losing repetitions
blocks.prompt: Find the monic polynomial in \(y\) whose roots are the squares of the roots of \(x^{3} - 4 x^{2} - x + 4=0\), counting multiplicity.
blocks.hint: Retain a factor for every original root position, even when two images coincide.
blocks.solution:
The polynomial factors as \(\left(x - 4\right) \left(x - 1\right) \left(x + 1\right)\). In particular the roots \(1\) and \(-1\) have the same square.

Their squares are \(1\), \(1\) and \(16\). The first value occurs twice.

Multiply the factors \(\left(y - 16\right) \left(y - 1\right)^{2}\), obtaining \(y^{3} - 18 y^{2} + 33 y - 16\). An alternative without factorisation is to replace \(x^2\) by \(y\) in \(-P(x)P(-x)\).

sections.title: What if the new roots involve high powers?
sections.label: Reduce the power at a root
sections.intro: Each old root satisfies the polynomial equation. Use that relation to simplify an expression before substituting into the original.

blocks.html: At a root of \(x^3+ax+b=0\), the value of \(x^3\) is \(-ax-b\). If \(a\ne0\) the new rule for the cube is linear on the root set.

blocks.title: Use the root equation to reduce a cubic expression
blocks.prompt: The cubic \(x^{3} + 3 x - 2=0\) has three roots, counted with multiplicity. Find the monic polynomial in \(y\) whose roots are their cubes.
blocks.hint: Replace the cube by the lower-degree expression before looking for the inverse.
blocks.solution:
At a root, \(x^3=2 - 3 x\). Thus the transformation is effectively linear on these three roots.

Set \(y=2 - 3 x\) and rearrange to obtain \(x=\frac{2}{3} - \frac{y}{3}\).

Substitute into the original cubic and multiply by \(-27\) to obtain \(y^{3} - 6 y^{2} + 39 y - 8\).

blocks.html: This simplification is true at the roots. It is not a polynomial identity valid at every x.

sections.title: Which values can a fractional transformation exclude?
sections.label: Check each denominator
sections.intro: A nonlinear rule can have a pole at an original input or an excluded value in its inverse. Write both conditions before cross-multiplying.

blocks.html: Check the old polynomial at the original pole, then test the value forbidden in the inverse in the final polynomial. Verify the degree after clearing denominators.

blocks.title: Check both excluded values of a fractional rule
blocks.prompt: For roots of \(x^{3} - 4 x^{2} - 11 x + 30=0\), use \(y=\frac{x - 1}{x - 4}\) to form the monic polynomial in \(y\). Also give the excluded value of \(y\) used in the inverse.
blocks.hint: Rearrange the fractional rule first, then check the old denominator and the new one separately.
blocks.solution:
Substituting \(x=4\) into the original gives \(-14\), which is non-zero. The pole does not belong to the original roots.

Rearrange to get \(x=\frac{4 y - 1}{y - 1}\), requiring \(y\ne1\).

Substitute, multiply by \((y-1)^3\) and normalise to obtain \(y^{3} - \frac{57 y^{2}}{14} + \frac{8}{7}\). At \(y=1\) its value is \(- \frac{27}{14}\), so no pole was introduced.

blocks.html: An excluded value never becomes an accepted root merely because formal denominators have disappeared.

blocks.title: Check both excluded values of a fractional rule
blocks.prompt: For roots of \(x^{3} - 10 x^{2} + 23 x - 14=0\), use \(y=\frac{x + 3}{x - 5}\) to form the monic polynomial in \(y\). Also give the excluded value of \(y\) used in the inverse.
blocks.hint: Rearrange the fractional rule first, then check the old denominator and the new one separately.
blocks.solution:
Substituting \(x=5\) into the original gives \(-24\), which is non-zero. The pole does not belong to the original roots.

Rearrange to get \(x=\frac{5 y + 3}{y - 1}\), requiring \(y\ne1\).

Substitute, multiply by \((y-1)^3\) and normalise to obtain \(y^{3} - \frac{7 y^{2}}{3} - \frac{35 y}{3} - \frac{25}{3}\). At \(y=1\) its value is \(- \frac{64}{3}\), so no pole was introduced.

blocks.html: State why the degree and multiplicities agree when the transformation is one-to-one on the original roots.

examples.title: Use the inverse affine substitution
examples.question: Let the old roots belong to \(x^{3} - 3 x^{2} - 6 x + 8=0\). Find the monic polynomial in \(y\) for the transformed roots defined by \(y=3 - 2 x\).
solution: Rearrange the rule for the original variable: \(x=\frac{3}{2} - \frac{y}{2}\).
Substitute this into the old polynomial, then multiply by \(-8\) to restore the monic leading coefficient.
Expansion gives \(y^{3} - 3 y^{2} - 33 y + 35\). Each new root comes from exactly one old root because the multiplier \(-2\) is non-zero.

examples.title: Reverse coefficients after checking zero
examples.question: For the roots of \(x^{3} - 3 x^{2} - 6 x + 8=0\), find the monic polynomial in \(y\) whose roots are their reciprocals.
solution: The original constant is non-zero. Put \(y=\frac1x\) so \(x=\frac1y\).
Multiplication by \(y^3\) gives \(8 y^{3} - 6 y^{2} - 3 y + 1=0\). The new constant is non-zero, so the excluded value \(y=0\) is not added.
Divide by \(8\) to obtain the monic polynomial \(y^{3} - \frac{3 y^{2}}{4} - \frac{3 y}{8} + \frac{1}{8}\).

examples.title: Square roots without losing repetitions
examples.question: Find the monic polynomial in \(y\) whose roots are the squares of the roots of \(x^{3} - 3 x^{2} - 4 x + 12=0\), counting multiplicity.
solution: The polynomial factors as \(\left(x - 3\right) \left(x - 2\right) \left(x + 2\right)\). In particular the roots \(2\) and \(-2\) have the same square.
Their squares are \(4\), \(4\) and \(9\). The first value occurs twice.
Multiply the factors \(\left(y - 9\right) \left(y - 4\right)^{2}\), obtaining \(y^{3} - 17 y^{2} + 88 y - 144\). An alternative without factorisation is to replace \(x^2\) by \(y\) in \(-P(x)P(-x)\).

examples.title: Square roots without losing repetitions
examples.question: Find the monic polynomial in \(y\) whose roots are the squares of the roots of \(x^{3} - 2 x^{2} - 16 x + 32=0\), counting multiplicity.
solution: The polynomial factors as \(\left(x - 4\right) \left(x - 2\right) \left(x + 4\right)\). In particular the roots \(4\) and \(-4\) have the same square.
Their squares are \(16\), \(16\) and \(4\). The first value occurs twice.

Multiply the factors \(\left(y - 16\right)^{2} \left(y - 4\right)\), obtaining \(y^{3} - 36 y^{2} + 384 y - 1024\). An alternative without factorisation is to replace \(x^2\) by \(y\) in \(-P(x)P(-x)\).

examples.title: Use the root equation to reduce a cubic expression
examples.question: The cubic \(x^{3} + 2 x + 3=0\) has three roots, counted with multiplicity. Find the monic polynomial in \(y\) whose roots are their cubes.
solution: At a root, \(x^3=- 2 x - 3\). Thus the transformation is effectively linear on these three roots.
Set \(y=- 2 x - 3\) and rearrange to obtain \(x=- \frac{y}{2} - \frac{3}{2}\).
Substitute into the original cubic and multiply by \(-8\) to obtain \(y^{3} + 9 y^{2} + 35 y + 27\).

examples.title: Check both excluded values of a fractional rule
examples.question: For roots of \(x^{3} - 3 x^{2} - 6 x + 8=0\), use \(y=\frac{x + 2}{x - 3}\) to form the monic polynomial in \(y\). Also give the excluded value of \(y\) used in the inverse.
solution: Substituting \(x=3\) into the original gives \(-10\), which is non-zero. The pole does not belong to the original roots.
Rearrange to get \(x=\frac{3 y + 2}{y - 1}\), requiring \(y\ne1\).
Substitute, multiply by \((y-1)^3\) and normalise to obtain \(y^{3} - \frac{9 y^{2}}{2} - 9 y\). At \(y=1\) its value is \(- \frac{25}{2}\), so no pole was introduced.

examples.title: Check both excluded values of a fractional rule
examples.question: For roots of \(x^{3} - 8 x^{2} + 9 x + 18=0\), use \(y=\frac{x + 1}{x - 2}\) to form the monic polynomial in \(y\). Also give the excluded value of \(y\) used in the inverse.
solution: Substituting \(x=2\) into the original gives \(12\), which is non-zero. The pole does not belong to the original roots.
Rearrange to get \(x=\frac{2 y + 1}{y - 1}\), requiring \(y\ne1\).
Substitute, multiply by \((y-1)^3\) and normalise to obtain \(y^{3} - \frac{23 y^{2}}{4} + 7 y\). At \(y=1\) its value is \(\frac{9}{4}\), so no pole was introduced.

extraPractice.title: Use the inverse affine substitution
extraPractice.prompt: Let the old roots belong to \(x^{3} - 8 x^{2} + 9 x + 18=0\). Find the monic polynomial in \(y\) for the transformed roots defined by \(y=4 - x\).
extraPractice.hint: Substitute for x, not for y. Clear constant denominators at the end.
extraPractice.solution:
Rearrange the rule for the original variable: \(x=4 - y\).

Substitute this into the old polynomial, then multiply by \(-1\) to restore the monic leading coefficient.

Expansion gives \(y^{3} - 4 y^{2} - 7 y + 10\). Each new root comes from exactly one old root because the multiplier \(-1\) is non-zero.

extraPractice.title: Reverse coefficients after checking zero
extraPractice.prompt: For the roots of \(x^{3} - 8 x^{2} + 9 x + 18=0\), find the monic polynomial in \(y\) whose roots are their reciprocals.
extraPractice.hint: Each coefficient reverses its place after multiplication by the highest power of the new variable.
extraPractice.solution:
The original constant is non-zero. Put \(y=\frac1x\) so \(x=\frac1y\).

Multiplication by \(y^3\) gives \(18 y^{3} + 9 y^{2} - 8 y + 1=0\). The new constant is non-zero, so the excluded value \(y=0\) is not added.

Divide by \(18\) to obtain the monic polynomial \(y^{3} + \frac{y^{2}}{2} - \frac{4 y}{9} + \frac{1}{18}\).

extraPractice.title: Square roots without losing repetitions
extraPractice.prompt: Find the monic polynomial in \(y\) whose roots are the squares of the roots of \(x^{3} - 5 x^{2} - 9 x + 45=0\), counting multiplicity.
extraPractice.hint: Retain a factor for every original root position, even when two images coincide.
extraPractice.solution:
The polynomial factors as \(\left(x - 5\right) \left(x - 3\right) \left(x + 3\right)\). In particular the roots \(3\) and \(-3\) have the same square.

Their squares are \(9\), \(9\) and \(25\). The first value occurs twice.

Multiply the factors \(\left(y - 25\right) \left(y - 9\right)^{2}\), obtaining \(y^{3} - 43 y^{2} + 531 y - 2025\). An alternative without factorisation is to replace \(x^2\) by \(y\) in \(-P(x)P(-x)\).

extraPractice.title: Use the root equation to reduce a cubic expression
extraPractice.prompt: The cubic \(x^{3} + 4 x + 1=0\) has three roots, counted with multiplicity. Find the monic polynomial in \(y\) whose roots are their cubes.
extraPractice.hint: Replace the cube by the lower-degree expression before looking for the inverse.
extraPractice.solution:
At a root, \(x^3=- 4 x - 1\). Thus the transformation is effectively linear on these three roots.

Set \(y=- 4 x - 1\) and rearrange to obtain \(x=- \frac{y}{4} - \frac{1}{4}\).

Substitute into the original cubic and multiply by \(-64\) to obtain \(y^{3} + 3 y^{2} + 67 y + 1\).

extraPractice.title: Check both excluded values of a fractional rule
extraPractice.prompt: For roots of \(x^{3} - 2 x^{2} - 19 x + 20=0\), use \(y=\frac{x + 4}{x - 11}\) to form the monic polynomial in \(y\). Also give the excluded value of \(y\) used in the inverse.
extraPractice.hint: Rearrange the fractional rule first, then check the old denominator and the new one separately.
extraPractice.solution:
Substituting \(x=11\) into the original gives \(900\), which is non-zero. The pole does not belong to the original roots.

Rearrange to get \(x=\frac{11 y + 4}{y - 1}\), requiring \(y\ne1\).

Substitute, multiply by \((y-1)^3\) and normalise to obtain \(y^{3} + 2 y^{2} + \frac{3 y}{4}\). At \(y=1\) its value is \(\frac{15}{4}\), so no pole was introduced.

glossary.definition: The input variable in the original polynomial.
The image of an original root under the stated rule.
Writing the old variable in terms of the new one.
A value at which the denominator of the rule is zero.
How many original root positions contribute a factor, including repeated images.

related.title: Symmetric functions of roots and power sums

fp1_roots_mixed.description: Choose a useful coefficient relation or substitution for linked roots, reciprocal quartics, repeated factors and reality checks.

sections.title: How can a root pattern reduce the unknowns?
sections.label: Express all roots in two parameters
sections.intro: A pattern among the roots can reduce the number of parameters you have to find. Use the symmetric relations to determine those parameters.

blocks.html: For three arithmetic values write \(a-d,a,a+d\) with \(d>0\) when they are distinct. Their sum fixes the centre immediately.

blocks.title: Turn an arithmetic pattern into coefficient conditions
blocks.prompt: Three distinct roots of a monic cubic are in arithmetic progression. Their sum is \(18\) and the sum of pair products is \(92\). Find the positive common difference and the monic polynomial.
blocks.hint: The middle root is one third of the sum.
blocks.solution:
Write the roots as \(a-d,a,a+d\) with \(d>0\). The sum is \(3a\), giving \(a=6\).

The pair-product sum is \(3a^2-d^2\). Substitute to get \(d^2=16\), so \(d=4\).

Multiply the factors given by the three roots to get \(x^{3} - 18 x^{2} + 92 x - 120\).

blocks.html: The pair products are not just the product of the two end terms. Include the products with the centre as well.

sections.title: When can a reciprocal quartic become a quadratic?
sections.label: Use the symmetry in coefficients
sections.intro: For a quartic whose coefficients read the same in reverse, divide by \(x^2\) and look for matching inverse powers.

blocks.html: Put \(y=x+\frac1x\) and use \(x^2+\frac1{x^2}=y^2-2\). A real x requires \(y^2-4\ge0\) when you solve \(x^2-yx+1=0\).

blocks.title: Keep the reduced values that come from real x
blocks.prompt: Let \(x^{4} - 3 x^{3} - 2 x^{2} - 3 x + 1\) equal zero. Put \(y=x+\frac1x\). Find both reduced y-values and the number of distinct real x-roots.
blocks.hint: Use the quadratic discriminant in x after solving the equation in y.
blocks.solution:
The constant term is one, so division by \(x^2\) is allowed at the roots.

Use \(x^2+\frac1{x^2}=y^2-2\) to get \(y^{2} - 3 y - 4=0\). Thus the candidates are \(-1\) and \(4\).

The equation \(x^2-yx+1=0\) has two real roots if \(|y|>2\), one distinct real root if \(|y|=2\), and none otherwise. Applying this test gives \(2\) distinct real x-roots.

blocks.html: At \(y=\pm2\) the quadratic has only one distinct real root. Count it once if the question asks for distinct values.

sections.title: How do two equal pair sums simplify a quartic?
sections.label: Shift the centre before solving
sections.intro: If both pairs have the same sum, both have the same midpoint. Shifting that midpoint to zero produces pairs with opposite values.

blocks.html: The polynomial in the shifted variable has only even powers. Solve for its square, check that the square is non-negative for real roots, then recover the original variable.

blocks.title: Centre two pairs and solve a quadratic in a square
blocks.prompt: The quartic \(x^{4} - 12 x^{3} + 25 x^{2} + 66 x - 80=0\) has roots in pairs with equal pair sums. Substitute \(x=y + 3\) to find its two positive values of \(y^2\) and all original roots.
blocks.hint: A quadratic in y² gives two y-values for each strictly positive square.
blocks.solution:
Putting the centre at zero gives \(y^{4} - 29 y^{2} + 100=0\). The odd powers vanish.

Factor as \(\left(y - 5\right) \left(y - 2\right) \left(y + 2\right) \left(y + 5\right)\), so the values of \(y^2\) are \(4\) and \(25\).

Use both signs of each square root and translate by \(3\) to obtain \(-2,1,5,8\).

blocks.html: Solving for the square gives fewer values than solving for the root itself. Retain both signs where they are distinct.

blocks.title: Centre two pairs and solve a quadratic in a square
blocks.prompt: The quartic \(x^{4} - 16 x^{3} + 62 x^{2} + 16 x - 63=0\) has roots in pairs with equal pair sums. Substitute \(x=y + 4\) to find its two positive values of \(y^2\) and all original roots.
blocks.hint: A quadratic in y² gives two y-values for each strictly positive square.
blocks.solution:
Putting the centre at zero gives \(y^{4} - 34 y^{2} + 225=0\). The odd powers vanish.

Factor as \(\left(y - 5\right) \left(y - 3\right) \left(y + 3\right) \left(y + 5\right)\), so the values of \(y^2\) are \(9\) and \(25\).

Use both signs of each square root and translate by \(4\) to obtain \(-1,1,7,9\).

sections.title: What can a sum of squares tell me about reality?
sections.label: Use a necessary condition
sections.intro: Suppose every root is real. A sum of their squares would then be non-negative, even when individual roots have different signs.

blocks.html: Compute \(S_2\) from coefficients. A negative answer contradicts that assumption and shows some roots are non-real.

blocks.title: Use a negative square sum to rule out four real roots
blocks.prompt: Can every root of \(x^{4} + x^{3} + 5 x^{2} + 3 x - 2=0\) be real? Find \(S_2\) and decide.
blocks.hint: A sum of squares is non-negative only when each squared quantity is real.
blocks.solution:
The monic coefficients give \(S_1=-1\) and \(\sum\alpha\beta=5\).

Thus \(S_2=-9\) by the square-sum identity.

If all roots were real, each square would be non-negative. The computed negative value rules that out.

blocks.html: A positive sum of squares is only a necessary-condition check. It does not prove that every root is real.

sections.title: What if each of two values occurs twice?
sections.label: Use a squared quadratic
sections.intro: When each of two distinct values occurs twice, halve the total root sum and square sum to recover the corresponding quantities for the two distinct values.

blocks.html: Write the quadratic with those two values as its roots. Squaring it gives the monic quartic with correct multiplicities.

blocks.title: Use two double roots to reconstruct a quartic
blocks.prompt: A monic quartic has two distinct real roots, each repeated twice. Its root sum is \(4\) and \(S_2=20\). Find the monic quadratic with the two distinct roots and the original monic quartic.
blocks.hint: Count each root twice in the given sums; count each root once in the quadratic.
blocks.solution:
Let the roots be \(u,u,v,v\). Hence \(u+v=2\) and \(u^2+v^2=10\).

Subtract the last quantity from \((u+v)^2\) and divide by two to get \(uv=-3\). The quadratic is \(x^{2} - 2 x - 3\).

Square that quadratic because both roots are repeated. Expansion yields \(x^{4} - 4 x^{3} - 2 x^{2} + 12 x + 9\).

blocks.html: Halving the quartic pair-product sum does not produce the product of the distinct roots. Use the square-sum identity.

blocks.title: Use two double roots to reconstruct a quartic
blocks.prompt: A monic quartic has two distinct real roots, each repeated twice. Its root sum is \(16\) and \(S_2=80\). Find the monic quadratic with the two distinct roots and the original monic quartic.
blocks.hint: Count each root twice in the given sums; count each root once in the quadratic.
blocks.solution:
Let the roots be \(u,u,v,v\). Hence \(u+v=8\) and \(u^2+v^2=40\).

Subtract the last quantity from \((u+v)^2\) and divide by two to get \(uv=12\). The quadratic is \(x^{2} - 8 x + 12\).

Square that quadratic because both roots are repeated. Expansion yields \(x^{4} - 16 x^{3} + 88 x^{2} - 192 x + 144\).

examples.title: Turn an arithmetic pattern into coefficient conditions
examples.question: Three distinct roots of a monic cubic are in arithmetic progression. Their sum is \(15\) and the sum of pair products is \(71\). Find the positive common difference and the monic polynomial.
solution: Write the roots as \(a-d,a,a+d\) with \(d>0\). The sum is \(3a\), giving \(a=5\).
The pair-product sum is \(3a^2-d^2\). Substitute to get \(d^2=4\), so \(d=2\).
Multiply the factors given by the three roots to get \(x^{3} - 15 x^{2} + 71 x - 105\).

examples.title: Keep the reduced values that come from real x
examples.question: Let \(x^{4} - 4 x^{3} + 5 x^{2} - 4 x + 1\) equal zero. Put \(y=x+\frac1x\). Find both reduced y-values and the number of distinct real x-roots.
solution: The constant term is one, so division by \(x^2\) is allowed at the roots.
Use \(x^2+\frac1{x^2}=y^2-2\) to get \(y^{2} - 4 y + 3=0\). Thus the candidates are \(1\) and \(3\).
The equation \(x^2-yx+1=0\) has two real roots if \(|y|>2\), one distinct real root if \(|y|=2\), and none otherwise. Applying this test gives \(2\) distinct real x-roots.

examples.title: Centre two pairs and solve a quadratic in a square
examples.question: The quartic \(x^{4} - 8 x^{3} + 7 x^{2} + 36 x - 36=0\) has roots in pairs with equal pair sums. Substitute \(x=y + 2\) to find its two positive values of \(y^2\) and all original roots.
solution: Putting the centre at zero gives \(y^{4} - 17 y^{2} + 16=0\). The odd powers vanish.
Factor as \(\left(y - 4\right) \left(y - 1\right) \left(y + 1\right) \left(y + 4\right)\), so the values of \(y^2\) are \(1\) and \(16\).
Use both signs of each square root and translate by \(2\) to obtain \(-2,1,3,6\).

examples.title: Centre two pairs and solve a quadratic in a square
examples.question: The quartic \(x^{4} + 4 x^{3} - 7 x^{2} - 22 x + 24=0\) has roots in pairs with equal pair sums. Substitute \(x=y - 1\) to find its two positive values of \(y^2\) and all original roots.
solution: Putting the centre at zero gives \(y^{4} - 13 y^{2} + 36=0\). The odd powers vanish.
Factor as \(\left(y - 3\right) \left(y - 2\right) \left(y + 2\right) \left(y + 3\right)\), so the values of \(y^2\) are \(4\) and \(9\).
Use both signs of each square root and translate by \(-1\) to obtain \(-4,-3,1,2\).

examples.title: Use a negative square sum to rule out four real roots
examples.question: Can every root of \(x^{4} + x^{3} + 4 x^{2} + x - 1=0\) be real? Find \(S_2\) and decide.
solution: The monic coefficients give \(S_1=-1\) and \(\sum\alpha\beta=4\).
Thus \(S_2=-7\) by the square-sum identity.
If all roots were real, each square would be non-negative. The computed negative value rules that out.

Square that quadratic because both roots are repeated. Expansion yields \(x^{4} - 4 x^{3} - 12 x^{2} + 32 x + 64\).

extraPractice.title: Keep the reduced values that come from real x
extraPractice.prompt: Let \(x^{4} + x^{3} - 4 x^{2} + x + 1\) equal zero. Put \(y=x+\frac1x\). Find both reduced y-values and the number of distinct real x-roots.
extraPractice.hint: Use the quadratic discriminant in x after solving the equation in y.
extraPractice.solution:
The constant term is one, so division by \(x^2\) is allowed at the roots.

Use \(x^2+\frac1{x^2}=y^2-2\) to get \(y^{2} + y - 6=0\). Thus the candidates are \(-3\) and \(2\).

extraPractice.solution:
Putting the centre at zero gives \(y^{4} - 52 y^{2} + 576=0\). The odd powers vanish.

Factor as \(\left(y - 6\right) \left(y - 4\right) \left(y + 4\right) \left(y + 6\right)\), so the values of \(y^2\) are \(16\) and \(36\).

Use both signs of each square root and translate by \(1\) to obtain \(-5,-3,5,7\).

extraPractice.title: Use a negative square sum to rule out four real roots
extraPractice.prompt: Can every root of \(x^{4} + x^{3} + 6 x^{2} + 4 x - 3=0\) be real? Find \(S_2\) and decide.
extraPractice.hint: A sum of squares is non-negative only when each squared quantity is real.
extraPractice.solution:
The monic coefficients give \(S_1=-1\) and \(\sum\alpha\beta=6\).

Thus \(S_2=-11\) by the square-sum identity.

If all roots were real, each square would be non-negative. The computed negative value rules that out.

extraPractice.title: Use two double roots to reconstruct a quartic
extraPractice.prompt: A monic quartic has two distinct real roots, each repeated twice. Its root sum is \(-4\) and \(S_2=20\). Find the monic quadratic with the two distinct roots and the original monic quartic.
extraPractice.hint: Count each root twice in the given sums; count each root once in the quadratic.
extraPractice.solution:
Let the roots be \(u,u,v,v\). Hence \(u+v=-2\) and \(u^2+v^2=10\).

Subtract the last quantity from \((u+v)^2\) and divide by two to get \(uv=-3\). The quadratic is \(x^{2} + 2 x - 3\).

Square that quadratic because both roots are repeated. Expansion yields \(x^{4} + 4 x^{3} - 2 x^{2} - 12 x + 9\).
